The salary calculator also works in reverse. Enter an hourly wage, your weekly hours and your paid weeks to find annual pay, or choose another pay period to convert that amount. Share Interactive — edit any field How the Salary Conversion Works The salary calculator first turns the pay amount you enter into annual gross pay. For an hourly amount, it multiplies the hourly rate by hours per week and weeks per year. To convert an annual salary back to an hourly rate, it divides annual pay by hours per week times weeks per year. A $52,000 salary spread across 2,080 work hours gives $25.00 an hour. The period you select tells the calculator how to interpret your pay amount. You can enter pay by the hour, day, week, every two weeks, half month, month or year. It then shows an hourly headline rate alongside annual, monthly, twice-a-month, every-two-weeks, weekly and daily amounts. Enter the hours and days you work so the time-based amounts use your schedule rather than the starting values. Monthly pay is annual pay divided by 12. Twice-a-month pay is annual pay divided by 24. Every-two-weeks pay divides annual pay by half the number of paid weeks, which means 26 checks across 52 paid weeks. Daily pay divides annual pay by days worked per week times weeks per year. The starting schedule of 40 hours across 52 weeks produces 2,080 hours because 40 multiplied by 52 equals 2,080. Change either input when a pay offer uses a different schedule. For instance, a $60,000 salary works out to $28.85 an hour across 52 paid weeks at 40 hours a week. Across 50 paid weeks at the same weekly hours, the hourly figure is $30.00. The calculator uses the paid weeks you enter. It does not model unpaid leave separately. You can start with a monthly or biweekly amount instead of annual pay. An hourly offer also responds to a change in weekly hours: $30 an hour at 37.5 hours a week gives $58,500 a year and $4,875.00 a month when you enter 52 paid weeks. Overtime, bonuses, unpaid leave and benefits are not modeled. If you are paid overtime or commission, enter an average pay amount and average hours for the conversion. Keep any comparison on the same basis. Bonuses are not modeled, so account for them separately when comparing pay offers. Anyone who needs an after-tax figure should use the paycheck calculator instead of treating the gross result as take-home pay. The hourly answer also changes when you work more hours, have fewer paid weeks or earn overtime, so update the inputs when those parts of an offer differ. At 40 hours across 52 weeks, the hourly rate is $28.85. Does this salary calculator include overtime? No. The salary calculator converts the pay amount and work schedule you enter without modeling separate overtime pay. That is $1,938.08 per biweekly paycheck after federal income tax and payroll tax. The paycheck calculator above starts with annual gross pay and biweekly checks, but you can enter pay per paycheck and choose a different schedule. It shows take-home pay per check as the headline result, with each deduction shown per check and per year. The result estimates annual federal tax liability for a W-2 employee who takes the standard deduction. It does not predict the exact amount an employer will withhold. For the worked example, enter $60,000 in annual gross pay, choose single filing and leave pre-tax retirement at $0. The standard deduction leaves $43,900 of taxable income. Federal income tax comes to $5,020, while Social Security takes $3,720 and Medicare takes $870. Together, those payroll taxes are $4,590. Subtract federal and payroll tax from gross pay to get $50,390 for the year. Across 26 biweekly checks, that is $1,938.08 per check, or 84.0% of gross pay. State tax, credits and other withholding could change what appears on a pay stub. Share Interactive — edit any field How Take-Home Pay Is Calculated The paycheck calculator estimates annual take-home pay, then divides it by the number of checks in your pay schedule. Annual take-home pay equals gross pay minus pre-tax retirement contributions, federal income tax, Social Security and Medicare. For the $60,000 single-filer example, the result is $50,390 a year and $1,938.08 across 26 biweekly checks. You can enter gross pay by year or by paycheck. The schedule choices are weekly, every two weeks, twice a month and monthly, with 52, 26, 24 and 12 checks respectively. If you need to convert a pay figure before entering it, use the salary calculator . Federal income tax starts with taxable income: gross pay minus your annual pre-tax retirement contribution and the standard deduction, with a floor of zero. The calculator applies the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) 2026 brackets band by band to that amount. For a single filer earning $60,000, taxable income is $43,900. The first $12,400 is taxed at 10%, producing $1,240. The remaining $31,500 is taxed at 12%, producing $3,780. Those bands add up to $5,020 in federal income tax. Being in a higher bracket does not apply that bracket's rate to every dollar of taxable income. Social Security is 6.2% of gross wages up to the $184,500 wage base. Medicare is 1.45% of all gross wages, with an additional 0.9% withheld on wages above $200,000. These payroll taxes use gross wages even when a pre-tax retirement contribution lowers taxable income. For example, Social Security on a $300,000 salary stops at $11,439, while Medicare comes to $5,250. On a $250,000 salary, Medicare is $4,075, including $450 in Additional Medicare withholding. The calculator shows Social Security and Medicare separately. A pre-tax retirement contribution lowers the income used to calculate federal income tax, but it does not lower the gross wages used for Social Security or Medicare. On a $100,000 single-filer salary, a $10,000 contribution reduces federal income tax from $13,170 to $10,970. Social Security stays at $6,200, and Medicare stays at $1,450. Annual take-home pay is $71,380 with the contribution, compared with $79,180 without it. The contribution lowers take-home pay by $7,800 because federal income tax falls by $2,200. Enter the contribution as an annual amount, even if you enter gross pay per paycheck. 2026 Federal Figures Used The paycheck calculator uses the following 2026 standard deductions, income tax brackets and payroll tax figures. Item 2026 figure Source Standard deduction, single $16,100 IRS 2026 adjustments Standard deduction, married filing jointly $32,200 IRS 2026 adjustments Standard deduction, head of household $24,150 IRS 2026 adjustments Income tax rates 10%, 12%, 22%, 24%, 32%, 35%, 37% IRS Rev. Proc. 2025-32 Single, top of the 10% and 12% brackets $12,400 and $50,400 of taxable income IRS Rev. Proc. 2025-32 Social Security tax 6.2% up to $184,500 of wages IRS Topic 751 Medicare tax 1.45% of all wages IRS Topic 751 Additional Medicare withholding 0.9% of wages above $200,000 IRS Topic 751 For more detail on where taxable income falls, use the federal tax bracket calculator . The figures above were checked on the linked IRS pages on 2026-11-15. Take-Home Pay at Different Salaries In our internal modeling, we ran 2026 federal brackets and payroll tax across salaries from $40,000 to $150,000 to estimate take-home pay. The table assumes a single filer taking the standard deduction, with no state tax, retirement contribution or other deductions. Each biweekly figure spreads the annual estimate across 26 checks. These figures are modeled results, so your entries in the paycheck calculator above may produce different amounts. Gross salary Federal income tax Social Security Medicare Take-home per year Take-home per biweekly check Share of gross $40,000 $2,620 $2,480 $580 $34,320 $1,320.00 85.8% $60,000 $5,020 $3,720 $870 $50,390 $1,938.08 84.0% $100,000 $13,170 $6,200 $1,450 $79,180 $3,045.38 79.2% $150,000 $24,734 $9,300 $2,175 $113,791 $4,376.58 75.9% The take-home share falls from 85.8% to 75.9% across the table as more taxable income reaches higher brackets. Social Security stops applying once wages reach $184,500. Pre-tax retirement can change the income-tax part of the result: a $10,000 contribution lowers take-home pay by $7,800 in the $100,000 single-filer case. Filing status changes the estimate too. At $60,000, married filing jointly produces $52,570 in annual take-home pay, or $2,021.92 per biweekly check. Head of household at $60,000 produces $51,462 annually and $1,979.31 per biweekly check. Choose the filing status that applies to the estimate you want to see. Married filing separately is not offered. What This Estimate Leaves Out The paycheck calculator leaves out taxes, deductions and withholding choices that can change the amount on an actual pay stub. State and local income tax. Tax credits, including the child tax credit. Itemized deductions. Health premiums, health savings account (HSA) contributions and other pre-tax items. Extra withholding requested on Form W-4. Tips, overtime, senior and qualified business income (QBI) deductions. This is an annual-liability estimate using the standard deduction. It does not calculate withholding under IRS Publication 15-T. An employer's actual check can therefore differ from the calculator's per-check figure. The calculator models 0.9% Additional Medicare withholding above $200,000 for every filing status. Final Additional Medicare liability uses different thresholds, including $250,000 for married filing jointly, as explained in IRS Topic 560 . A married couple's final liability can therefore differ from the Additional Medicare amount withheld. This paycheck calculator is not suited to self-employed or 1099 income, multiple jobs or itemized deductions. Use figures that account for those circumstances instead. State tax, credits or extra W-4 withholding would also change the answer, so treat the result as an estimate rather than personalized withholding advice. Enter your gross pay and filing status in the paycheck calculator above, then compare its result with your pay stub. Frequently asked questions How much of my paycheck will I keep after taxes? At $60,000 a year, a single filer keeps an estimated $50,390 before state tax. That is $1,938.08 per biweekly check, or 84.0% of gross pay. The estimate subtracts federal income tax, Social Security and Medicare. Enter your own pay in the calculator above because filing status and pre-tax retirement contributions can change the result. Is a paycheck calculator accurate? It is an estimate of annual federal tax liability and take-home pay under the listed assumptions. It uses the standard deduction and does not calculate an employer's exact withholding under IRS Publication 15-T. State tax, credits and health premiums are also left out. Compare the per-check result with a pay stub if you need to understand a difference. How do I calculate my paycheck manually? Start with annual gross pay and subtract pre-tax retirement contributions and the standard deduction to find taxable income. Apply the federal brackets to taxable income band by band. Then subtract federal income tax, Social Security, Medicare and the retirement contribution from gross pay. Divide annual take-home pay by the number of checks in your chosen pay schedule. Does this paycheck calculator include state tax? No. The paycheck calculator does not subtract state or local income tax. Its take-home figure is therefore before those taxes. If state or local tax appears on your pay stub, that is one reason the actual net check can be lower than this estimate. Why is my real paycheck different from this estimate? Your employer's withholding can differ from this annual-liability estimate. The calculator also leaves out state tax, credits, health premiums and extra W-4 withholding. It does not model tips or overtime deductions. Compare the deduction rows with your pay stub to identify which amounts the estimate leaves out. How does a 401(k) contribution change my take-home pay? A pre-tax retirement contribution reduces the income used for federal income tax, while Social Security and Medicare still use gross wages. In the $100,000 single-filer case, a $10,000 contribution lowers federal income tax by $2,200. Take-home pay falls by $7,800 rather than the full contribution amount. Enter your annual contribution to see the change in the calculator. Why does Social Security tax stop on high salaries? Social Security tax applies only up to the 2026 wage base of $184,500. The employee rate is 6.2%, so the modeled Social Security tax on a $300,000 salary is $11,439. Medicare still applies to gross wages above the Social Security wage base. The calculator shows both taxes separately in its results. Does a paycheck calculator include Medicare tax? Yes. This paycheck calculator subtracts Medicare tax at 1.45% of gross wages. It also models an extra 0.9% withheld on wages above $200,000. Final Additional Medicare liability can use a different threshold for married filing jointly, so that withholding estimate may differ from the final tax. The tax bracket calculator above finds your taxable income by subtracting a deduction from your income before deductions. It uses the standard deduction unless you enter your own total. Add your filing status to see your 2026 federal bracket, estimated tax and effective rate, plus the room left before the next bracket starts. For example, take a single filer with $85,000 of income and the $16,100 standard deduction. Taxable income is $68,900, so the top dollars land in the 22% bracket and the tax comes to $9,870. That is an effective rate of 11.6%, with $36,800 of room before the 24% bracket starts. Share Interactive — edit any field How it works The calculator subtracts the standard deduction, or a custom itemized total you enter, from your income before deductions to get taxable income, which never goes below zero. The 2026 standard deduction is $16,100 for a single filer and for married filing separately. It is $32,200 for married filing jointly and $24,150 for head of household, and your filing status also sets where each bracket starts. Tax is figured band by band, so only the dollars inside each band are taxed at that band's rate. For the single filer in the example above, the first $12,400 of taxable income is taxed at 10%, which is $1,240. The next $38,000 is taxed at 12%, which adds $4,560. The last $18,500 is taxed at 22% for $4,070, and that top band sets the marginal rate, which is the rate of the highest band holding any taxable dollar. The effective rate divides total tax by income before deductions, so $9,870 on $85,000 comes to 11.6%. Room left is the taxable income you can add before the next bracket starts, which is $36,800 here because the 24% band begins at $105,700. A married couple filing jointly with $150,000 of income lands in the 22% bracket at an effective rate of 10.2%. A head of household with $60,000 of income owes $3,948 and sits in the 12% bracket. A single filer with $250,000 of income reaches the 32% bracket, but the effective rate is 20.5%. The calculator applies ordinary-income brackets only, so it leaves out credits, capital gains rates, the qualified business income deduction, payroll tax and state tax. It is the wrong tool if you need a full return, owe self-employment tax or have capital gains, and ordinary income vs capital gains tax covers capital gains rates. A bigger deduction or a different filing status changes the result, so rerun the calculator with those inputs, then read the guide on how much tax you will owe . Frequently asked questions What tax bracket am I in? Your bracket is the rate on your last dollar of taxable income, which is your income after the deduction. A single filer with $85,000 of income has $68,900 of taxable income and lands in the 22% bracket. Enter your own income and filing status in the calculator above to see yours. How do you calculate your tax bracket? Subtract your deduction from your income, then find the band that holds your last taxable dollar. For a single filer, the 22% band covers taxable income over $50,400 up to $105,700. The calculator above does both steps and names the bracket for you. What is the difference between a marginal and an effective tax rate? The marginal rate is the rate on your last taxable dollar, and the effective rate is your total tax divided by income before deductions. A single filer with $85,000 of income has a 22% marginal rate. The same filer's effective rate is 11.6%, because $9,870 of tax is spread across all $85,000. Does moving into a higher bracket mean all my income is taxed more? No. Only the dollars inside the higher band are taxed at the higher rate. A single filer whose taxable income rises past $105,700 pays 24% on the dollars above that line. The tax on every dollar below $105,700 stays the same. What are the 2026 federal tax brackets? The 2026 federal rates run from 10% to 37% across seven brackets. For a single filer, the top 37% rate starts above $640,600 of taxable income. The 2026 tax brackets guide lists every threshold for each filing status, and the projected 2027 brackets cover the following year. The figures come from the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) Revenue Procedure for the 2026 tax year . What is the standard deduction for 2026? The 2026 standard deduction is $16,100 for a single filer. It is also $16,100 for married filing separately, $32,200 for married filing jointly and $24,150 for head of household. The calculator uses it by default unless you enter a custom deduction. The amounts appear in the IRS release on the 2026 adjustments . How do I lower my taxable income to drop a bracket? In this calculator, a deduction larger than the standard deduction is what lowers taxable income. A single filer with $68,900 of taxable income must get it to $50,400 or less to reach the 12% bracket. That takes $18,500 more in deductions, so enter a custom total above to test it. This page does not give personal tax advice. Does this calculator include state tax? No. The calculator covers federal ordinary-income brackets only, with no state tax. It also leaves out payroll tax, credits, capital gains rates and the qualified business income deduction. Add your state tax separately, and browse all calculators for other money tools. To estimate your take-home pay after payroll tax, use the paycheck calculator. Sources We prioritize primary sources for rules, formulas, rates, limits, and definitions.
